lessons.title: Knife Anatomy: Point, Edge, Spine, and Tang
lessons.body: A knife is made of distinct parts, each with a job. The point is the sharp tip, used for piercing. The edge is the sharpened cutting side. The spine is the thick, unsharpened back of the blade, giving strength. The tang is the part of the steel that extends into the handle. In Africa, you see these parts on a Moroccan koummya or a Congolese machete. The point can be dropped (curved down to the edge), clip (a notch on the spine), or spear (centered). The edge can be plain or serrated. The spine can be straight or curved. The tang can be full (extends all the way through the handle), half, or hidden (a stick tang). For a strong working knife, a full tang is best. For a light slicer, a half tang works. The handle scales (wood, bone, or horn) are attached to the tang with rivets or epoxy. In many African knives, the tang is burned into a wooden handle for a tight fit. Knowing these parts helps you design a knife that works. For example, a skinning knife needs a deep belly (curved edge) and a drop point. A bushcraft knife needs a strong spine for batoning (splitting wood). Measure the tang length to match your handle material. A typical full tang is 10â12 cm long. The spine thickness is usually 3â5 mm for a sturdy knife. The edge angle is about 20 degrees per side for general use. Start by sketching these parts on paper before you touch steel.

lessons.title: Designing a Blade: Profile and Dimensions
lessons.body: Before you cut steel, draw your blade profile on paper. Use graph paper or a cardboard template. The profile is the outline of the blade. Start with the overall length: a small knife is 15â18 cm, a medium knife 20â25 cm, a large knife 30â40 cm. For a general-purpose knife, 22 cm overall with a 10 cm blade works well. The blade width (from edge to spine) is typically 2.5â4 cm. The spine thickness is 3â5 mm. The point shape depends on use: a drop point for skinning, a clip point for utility, a spear point for piercing. The edge curve (belly) helps slicing. A straight edge is good for chopping. Draw the profile with a pencil, then cut it out and trace it onto a piece of mild steel or cardboard. Hold it in your hand to check the feel. Adjust the handle length: for a full-hand grip, the handle should be 10â12 cm long. The finger guard (if any) should be 1â2 cm. In Africa, you can use old leaf springs from cars (5160 steel) or files (1095 steel). These are good blade steels. Draw the profile so the grain of the steel runs lengthwise. Avoid sharp inside cornersâthey cause cracks. Round all curves. Once you are happy, cut the template from thin plywood or metal. This is your pattern. You will use it to mark steel. Keep the design simple for your first knife: a straight spine, a curved edge, and a drop point. That is easy to grind and works for many tasks.

lessons.title: Marking and Layout on Steel
lessons.body: To transfer your design to steel, you need a few tools: a scriber (or a sharp nail), a center punch, a hammer, a permanent marker, and layout fluid (or shoe polish, or a marker). Clean the steel with sandpaper or a rag. If using layout fluid, spray or brush a thin coat and let it dry. Otherwise, color the area with a permanent marker. Place your template on the steel and trace around it with your scriber. Use a center punch to mark any holes (for handle pins) and the start of the cutting line. For a full tang knife, mark the tang shape too. If you are making a hidden tang, mark the centerline of the tang. Double-check your measurements: blade length, handle length, and overall length. A common mistake is not leaving enough steel for the handle. Mark the plunge line (where the bevel starts) about 2â3 cm from the handle. Mark the edge centerline along the blade. Use a ruler to keep lines straight. For curved sections, use a French curve or a flexible ruler. If you are recycling a leaf spring, first anneal it (heat to 800Â°C and cool slowly in ash) to make it soft and easy to mark and cut. Mark on both sides if you can, or use a marker on one side and flip the steel to check alignment. Once marked, punch all holes. Now you are ready to cut. Remember: measure twice, cut once. In many African workshops, a simple scriber made from an old file works perfectly. Keep your lines visibleâre-mark if they rub off.

lessons.title: Cutting and Shaping the Profile
lessons.body: Cutting the profile from steel can be done with a hacksaw, an angle grinder, a plasma cutter, or a chisel and hammer (for thin steel). For most beginners, an angle grinder with a cut-off wheel is fastest. Clamp the steel securely to a workbench. Wear safety glasses, gloves, and ear protection. Cut along your marked line, leaving about 1â2 mm of extra steel. Do not cut exactly on the lineâyou will grind to the line later. For straight cuts, use a hacksaw with a 24 TPI blade. For curves, use an angle grinder or a die grinder with a carbide burr. If you have access to a bandsaw with a metal-cutting blade, that is ideal. After rough cutting, use a bench grinder or an angle grinder with a grinding wheel to shape the profile to your line. Keep the steel cool by dipping it in water frequentlyâoverheating can ruin the steel's hardness. For a professional look, file the edges smooth with a mill file. Check your progress often by holding the blade to the light or comparing to your template. For a hidden tang, cut the tang narrower than the blade. For a full tang, cut the handle shape as well. Once the profile is shaped, deburr all edges. If you are making a knife from a file, be careful not to overheat itâif it turns blue, you have lost hardness. In that case, you will need to re-heat-treat later. After cutting, your blade should match your template. Now you can move to grinding bevels. In rural Africa, many smiths use a simple hacksaw and files to cut and shape, which takes longer but works well.

lessons.title: Introduction to Grinding: Bevels and Plunge Lines
lessons.body: The bevel is the angled cut from the spine down to the edge. It creates the cutting edge. The plunge line is where the bevel stops near the handle. A clean plunge line looks professional and prevents cracks. To grind a bevel, you can use a belt grinder (best), an angle grinder, or a file. For beginners, a file is safe and cheap. Clamp the blade edge-up in a vise. Draw a line on the blade where you want the bevel to start (the plunge line). For a flat grind, file at a consistent angle, usually 4â8 degrees per side for a thin knife, or 10â15 degrees for a heavy chopper. Count your strokes and check often. For a scandi grind (popular in bushcraft), the bevel is a single flat angle of about 12â15 degrees per side. For a convex grind, use a belt grinder with a slack belt. The plunge line should be perpendicular to the edge or slightly angled. Use a file guide or a piece of angle iron to keep the file straight. Work slowly, alternating sides to keep the edge centered. Do not grind the edge too thinâleave about 0.5 mm for the final sharpening. If using a belt grinder, use a 60â120 grit belt for rough grinding, then 220â400 for refining. Keep a bucket of water nearby to cool the steel. Overheating will ruin the heat treatment. After grinding, the bevel should be even on both sides. Check by looking down the edge. A common mistake is grinding past the plunge line into the handle. Mark your plunge line clearly and stop there. In Africa, many smiths use a simple file jig made from wood and a clamp. Practice on scrap steel first.

lessons.title: Design Considerations for Function and Aesthetics
lessons.body: A good knife balances function and beauty. Function comes first: the knife must cut well, feel comfortable, and last. For function, consider the task. A chef's knife needs a thin, hard edge (60â62 HRC) and a comfortable handle. A machete needs a tough, soft edge (55â58 HRC) to resist chipping. A hunting knife needs a sharp point and a deep belly for skinning. The handle should fit your hand: not too thick, not too thin. For most hands, a handle circumference of 10â12 cm is good. Use materials that are available: hardwood (ebony, mahogany, olive), bone, horn, or even micarta made from cloth and resin. For aesthetics, you can add a brass guard, a mosaic pin, or a file-worked spine. But do not sacrifice strength for looks. A fancy handle that breaks is useless. In Africa, traditional knives often have carved handles and leather sheaths. You can incorporate local patterns or materials. For example, use a piece of warthog tusk for a handle. Or etch a pattern on the blade with vinegar and salt. The finish of the blade matters: a satin finish (400â800 grit) hides scratches, while a mirror polish (2000 grit) shows them. For a working knife, a satin finish is practical. The sheath should be designed to hold the knife safely. Leather or kydex works. Always test your knife: cut rope, carve wood, and check comfort. Adjust the design if needed. Remember, a knife is a toolâit should serve you well. But a beautiful knife brings pride. In your design, aim for a tool that works hard and looks good doing it.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Blade Design, Layout & Shaping for the African Workshop

This practical reference consolidates the six lessons in the Blade Design and Layout module into a single working document you can pin to the wall of your forge. It is written for the small-scale African bladesmith who is building a business â not a hobby â and who needs repeatable numbers, not vague advice. Whether you are forging from leaf-spring steel in Kumasi, stock-removing from an old saw blade in Nakuru, or grinding machetes in Lubumbashi, the geometry, layout and grinding principles below apply. Get them right and your knives will cut better, last longer, and sell at a higher margin.

1. Knife Anatomy: The Vocabulary of Value

Every knife you sell is judged by six anatomical features. Know them, and you can explain your price.

  • Point â the piercing end. The profile (clip, drop, spear, tanto) determines whether the knife is for skinning, slicing or stabbing.
  • Edge â the cutting geometry. A thin edge (15â20Â° per side) slices; a thick edge (25â30Â°) chops and batons.
  • Spine â the unsharpened back. It stiffens the blade and can be squared for fire-steel striking.
  • Tang â the extension of the blade into the handle. Full tang = strongest, most marketable; stick tang = lighter, traditional.
  • Ricasso & Plunge Line â the flat section above the edge and the transition into the bevel. Clean plunge lines signal craftsmanship.
  • Handle & Pins â scales, bolsters and fasteners. In African markets, hardwood (ebony, mvule, mukwa) and bone command premium prices.

2. Designing a Blade: Profile and Dimensions

Design on paper before you touch steel. A 1:1 drawing on card stock becomes your template â trace it onto every blank so your batch is consistent. Consistency is what turns a forge into a brand.

For the African market, four profiles cover 90% of demand:

  • Drop-point hunter â skinning and general bushcraft. Blade 100â130 mm, width 30â35 mm.
  • Machete / panga â agriculture and land clearing. Blade 400â600 mm, width 45â60 mm, edge 20â25Â°.
  • Chef's knife â urban kitchens, growing middle class. Blade 180â210 mm, width 45â50 mm.
  • Utility / paring â high-volume, low-cost sellers. Blade 80â100 mm, width 20â25 mm.

Keep the blade-to-handle ratio around 60:40 for hunters and 70:30 for machetes. A handle shorter than 100 mm will not fit a working hand; longer than 130 mm and you lose control.

3. Marking and Layout on Steel

Layout is where accuracy becomes profit. A mis-marked blank wastes steel, gas and grinding belts. Use a fine-tip layout dye (or a permanent marker), a scriber (an old hacksaw blade ground to a point works), and a steel rule. Mark centre lines first, then profile, then the plunge-line position.

Always work from a datum â one edge or the centre line â so errors do not compound. Mark both sides of the blank; flipping errors are the most common cause of asymmetric blades.

4. Cutting and Shaping the Profile

You have three realistic options in a small African workshop:

Table 1: Profile-cutting methods â cost, speed and suitability
MethodTypical cost (USD)SpeedBest forNotes
Hacksaw + files5â15Slow1â3 knives/weekNo power needed; excellent for learning
Angle grinder (115 mm)40â90Medium5â15 knives/weekMost common entry tool; watch heat
Bandsaw (portable)150â400Fast15â40 knives/weekNeeds reliable power or generator
Plasma / waterjet (outsourced)1â3 per blankVery fast50+ knives/weekUse a local engineering shop; keep a template

Source: Cost ranges compiled from tool prices in Kenya, Ghana and South Africa (2024 market surveys) and the American Bladesmith Society recommended beginner tool list.

Regardless of method, cut outside your line by 1â2 mm and grind back to it. This leaves room for heat and error. On a grinder, dip the steel in water every 3â5 seconds â if you can't touch it, you're burning the steel.

5. Introduction to Grinding: Bevels and Plunge Lines

The bevel is the knife's engine. There are three common grinds:

  • Flat grind â strongest, easiest to learn, best for machetes and working knives.
  • Scandi grind â zero-bevel, excellent for bushcraft; popular in Southern Africa.
  • Hollow grind â thinnest slicing geometry; requires a contact wheel; best for chef's knives.

The plunge line is where the bevel meets the ricasso. A crisp, vertical plunge line is the single clearest sign of a skilled maker. Establish it with the edge of your grinding belt, keep the blade perpendicular to the belt, and use a file guide (a hardened steel clamp) for your first 20 knives.

Table 2: Recommended edge angles by knife type and use
Knife typeEdge angle (per side)Included anglePrimary use
Chef's knife10â15Â°20â30Â°Slicing, chopping vegetables
Hunter / skinner15â20Â°30â40Â°Skinning, general bushcraft
Machete / panga20â25Â°40â50Â°Clearing brush, harvesting
Survival / chopper25â30Â°50â60Â°Batoning, heavy chopping

Source: Edge-angle ranges consistent with Caterpillar-style field-knife specifications, the Buck Knives sharpening guide, and the KnivesShipFree blade-geometry reference.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Grinding and Cutting

Angle grinders and belt grinders cause more workshop injuries than any other tool in a bladesmith's shop. Always wear impact-rated safety glasses, a face shield when grinding, hearing protection and a P2/N95 dust mask (metal dust and belt dust are carcinogenic). Never wear gloves near a spinning belt or wheel â they can catch and pull your hand in. Keep a bucket of clean water and a first-aid kit within arm's reach. Check your grinder's guard and disc rating before every session. In many African markets, cheap unrated cutting discs shatter â buy rated discs only, and never exceed the RPM stamped on the disc. If you run a generator, ensure it is earthed and that cables are not trailing through water.

6. Design Considerations for Function and Aesthetics

Function sells the first knife; aesthetics sell the second. Balance the two:

  • Function: match steel thickness to use (2 mm for paring, 4â5 mm for machetes); match handle material to climate (stabilised wood resists humidity better than raw ebony); match edge angle to task (see Table 2).
  • Aesthetics: a clean plunge line, even bevels, symmetrical handle pins and a hand-rubbed finish (400â800 grit) command 20â40% higher prices in urban African markets and for export.
  • Branding: stamp or etch your mark on the ricasso. A maker's mark turns a knife into a product and a product into a business.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. â Draw the profile 1:1 on card; confirm blade-to-handle ratio (60:40 hunter, 70:30 machete).
  2. â Mark centre line and profile on both sides of the blank with dye and scriber.
  3. â Cut 1â2 mm outside the line; never cut to the line.
  4. â Keep steel cool â dip every 3â5 seconds; if you can't touch it, stop.
  5. â Establish the plunge line with a file guide; keep the blade perpendicular to the belt.
  6. â Grind bevels to the angle in Table 2 for the intended use.
  7. â Check symmetry by eye and with a straight edge before heat treatment.
  8. â Wear eye, ear and respiratory protection; keep water and first-aid within reach.

Further Reading (free, official sources)

  • American Bladesmith Society â Bladesmithing curriculum and safety resources
  • Bladesmith's Forum â beginner tutorials on layout, grinding and plunge lines
  • OSHA Machine Guarding eTool â grinder safety fundamentals
  • NIIR Project Consultancy â small-scale metal products business profiles (India/Africa context)
  • FAO â agricultural tool design and local manufacturing guides

Business takeaway: In the African bladesmithing market, the makers who win are those who standardise. Draw once, template once, mark the same way every time, grind the same angles every time. Consistency reduces waste, shortens training time for apprentices, and lets you quote a price with confidence. Your layout table is your production line â treat it like one.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the tang on a knife?
options: B) To provide a sharp point
C) To extend into the handle for strength and attachment
D) To protect the user's hand
quiz.explanation: The tang is the part of the blade that extends into the handle, providing strength and a way to attach handle scales.

quiz.q: Which part of the knife is the unsharpened back edge?
quiz.explanation: The spine is the thick, unsharpened back of the blade that gives strength.

quiz.q: What is a full tang?
options: A) A tang that extends all the way through the handle
B) A tang that is half the length of the handle
C) A tang that is hidden inside the handle
D) A tang that is made of plastic
quiz.explanation: A full tang runs the entire length of the handle, providing maximum strength.

quiz.q: For a general-purpose knife, what is a typical overall length?
quiz.explanation: A medium knife of 22â25 cm overall is versatile for many tasks.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spine thickness for a sturdy knife?
quiz.explanation: A spine thickness of 3â5 mm provides a good balance of strength and weight.

quiz.q: Which steel is commonly recycled from cars for blades?
quiz.explanation: 5160 steel from leaf springs is a tough, popular choice for blades in Africa.

quiz.q: What should you use to mark steel before cutting?
options: B) A scriber or permanent marker
quiz.explanation: A scriber or permanent marker makes visible lines on steel that resist rubbing off.

quiz.q: Why should you leave 1â2 mm of extra steel when rough cutting?
options: A) To allow for grinding to the final line
B) To make the knife heavier
quiz.explanation: Leaving extra steel gives you room to grind precisely to your marked profile.

quiz.q: What is the plunge line?
options: A) The sharp edge of the knife
B) The line where the bevel stops near the handle
C) The curve of the blade
D) The hole for handle pins
quiz.explanation: The plunge line is where the bevel grind stops, usually near the handle.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for grinding bevels as a beginner?
quiz.explanation: A file is safe, cheap, and allows controlled grinding for beginners.

quiz.q: What is a scandi grind?
options: B) A single flat bevel of about 12â15 degrees per side
D) A double bevel of 20 degrees per side
quiz.explanation: A scandi grind is a single flat bevel, popular for bushcraft knives.

quiz.q: Why should you keep steel cool while grinding?
options: A) To prevent it from melting
B) To avoid losing heat treatment
C) To make it easier to grind
quiz.explanation: Overheating can ruin the steel's hardness, so cooling is essential.

quiz.q: What is the typical edge angle for a general-purpose knife?
quiz.explanation: A 20-degree per side edge angle is a good compromise for durability and sharpness.

quiz.q: Which handle material is commonly used in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Warthog tusk is a traditional and available material in many African regions.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a center punch?
options: B) To mark hole locations for drilling
quiz.explanation: A center punch creates a small indentation to guide a drill bit.

quiz.q: What is annealing?
options: A) Heating and cooling slowly to soften steel
B) Heating and quenching to harden steel
quiz.explanation: Annealing softens steel by heating and cooling slowly, making it easier to cut and shape.

quiz.q: Which part of the knife is the sharpened cutting side?
quiz.explanation: The edge is the sharpened side that does the cutting.

quiz.q: What is a hidden tang?
options: A) A tang that is visible on the outside
B) A tang that extends only partway into the handle
C) A tang that is hidden inside the handle
D) A tang made of wood
quiz.explanation: A hidden tang is enclosed within the handle material and not visible.

quiz.q: What is the recommended handle length for a full-hand grip?
quiz.explanation: A handle of 10â12 cm fits most adult hands comfortably.

quiz.q: What is a drop point blade shape good for?
quiz.explanation: The drop point has a curved edge that is excellent for skinning game.

quiz.q: What does HRC measure?
quiz.explanation: HRC (Rockwell C) measures the hardness of steel.

quiz.q: Which finish hides scratches better?
quiz.explanation: A satin finish (400â800 grit) is less likely to show scratches than a mirror polish.

quiz.q: What is the first step in designing a blade?
options: C) Draw the profile on paper
quiz.explanation: Drawing the profile on paper helps you plan before cutting steel.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a finger guard?
options: A) To make the knife look nice
B) To prevent the hand from slipping onto the blade
quiz.explanation: A finger guard protects the user's hand from slipping forward onto the edge.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common mistake when marking steel?
options: B) Not leaving enough steel for the handle
quiz.explanation: Forgetting to allow enough steel for the handle is a common error that ruins a knife.

quiz.q: What is the best way to cut curves in steel?
options: B) Angle grinder or die grinder
quiz.explanation: An angle grinder or die grinder with a cutting wheel can follow curves better than a hacksaw.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a file guide?
options: A) To hold the file at a consistent angle
quiz.explanation: A file guide helps maintain a consistent angle when filing bevels.

quiz.q: What is a common steel for beginner bladesmiths?
quiz.explanation: 1095 is a simple high-carbon steel that is easy to heat treat and sharpen.

quiz.q: Why is it important to round inside corners in a blade design?
options: A) To make it look better
B) To prevent cracks from stress
quiz.explanation: Sharp inside corners create stress points that can lead to cracks.

quiz.q: What is the final step before attaching a handle?
quiz.explanation: Heat treating hardens the blade and should be done before attaching the handle.
